articles.title: Michel Zecler: Police officers sentenced for beating of music producer
articles.summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
articles.body:
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

All were told they could never serve in the police again.

The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

articles.title: Rings of Power filming allows Morfydd Clark to see 'secret bits' of Wales
articles.summary: Rings of Power actress Morfydd Clark sees 'secret bits' of Wales in filming
articles.body:
Actress Morfydd Clark has described how filming Rings of Power allowed her to see "all these secret bits" of Wales she had not visited before.

The fantasy adventure is set thousands of years before the events of JRR Tolkien's The Hobbit and Lord of the Rings in the fictional Middle Earth.

Clark, who is from Penarth, Vale of Glamorgan, was able to see parts of her own country she had not explored before while filming the third series of the Amazon Prime Video programme.

The star is reprising her leading role as the fierce elf commander Galadriel - and has also admitted how she slipped some Welsh words into her role.

Clark said her mother used to wait for the credits to see the interesting places where programmes had been shot.

It is reported Rings of Power was filmed at Neath Abbey and Trefil Quarry, Blaenau Gwent, among other places.

Last autumn, the cast was also spotted in Devon , shooting along the coast.

"Look at the credits," Clark said, urging fans to do the same as her mum to find out where it was filmed.

It is not only the scenery that may be familiar to people from Wales, but Tolkien's invented Elvish language has been described as having Celtic influences .

Clark, a fluent Welsh speaker, admitted slipping some words in, including the command "cer" to her horse – the Welsh word for "go".

The actress, who has also starred in Dracula and His Dark Materials, warned fans that all is not well for the protagonists in the upcoming series, joking: "It's going terribly."

Referring to the evil sorcerer who is trying to take over the fictional Middle Earth, Clark said: "Sauron is back and powerful and evil.

"They're just desperately trying to stem the tide."

Series three is set five years after the events of series two, and hope is dim in Middle Earth as Sauron's armies have conquered almost all in their path.

A few pockets of resistance remain, including Galadriel and her fellow elves, but Sauron works day and night to harness the power of the One Ring to crush them.

Despite this, Clark says the series will also look back on Galadriel's happier days, where the audience will see the serious commander dance and be cheerful.

Clark enjoyed the chance to "go back in time" and explore this new side of her character, adding: "It felt really exciting to go and find a different part of who she was."

In Jackson's Lord of the Rings film trilogy, Galadriel is serene and wise yet immensely powerful.

Meanwhile, the Prime Video prequel depicts the character in her youth, wilful and rebellious.

"It's wonderful to play someone brave and unapologetic, and also not afraid of social consequences," Clark said.

"I like to try and push myself to be a bit more like her at times."

The Lord of the Rings franchise is globally beloved, so taking on such a recognised role as Galadriel comes with a lot of pressure, believes Clark.

However, given that an actor's job is to "make a career out of emotions", she feels a similar responsibility in all her acting pursuits.

"I've just resigned myself to the fact the neurosis will always be there, whether I'm doing a speech at Christmas or filming this," she said.

Series three of Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is available to watch now.

articles.title: Birds die in blaze at one of largest foie gras farms in the US
articles.summary: Hundreds of young birds were also rescued from the fire, which comes as foie gras is under renewed scrutiny over animal welfare concerns.
articles.body:
A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.

The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.

Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.

Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.

Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.

"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.

The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.

Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.

The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.

Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.

Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.

New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.

At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.

Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

articles.title: Palisades arson retrial ends with conviction of man accused of sparking deadly wildfire
articles.summary: Jonathan Rinderknecht, a 30-year-old former Uber driver, was on trial for a second time after a jury over the summer deadlocked 10-2 in favor of his acquitta...
articles.body:
Following a mistrial over the summer, a federal jury on Friday convicted a 30-year-old former Uber driver accused of intentionally setting a blaze that later became the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.

Federal prosecutors accused Jonathan Rinderknecht of using a lighter to ignite the Lachman fire on Jan. 1, 2025 — a fire they said burned underground for days and reignited as the deadly Palisades fire. Rinderknecht's defense attorney argued there was no evidence proving his client set the fire and offered fireworks as an alternative cause.

The jury deliberated for just over two days before returning its verdict of guilty on both counts he faced. Rinderknecht's eyebrows shot up as the guilty outcome was announced.

Rinderknecht hugged his defense team after the verdict was read and the judge scheduled him to be sentenced on March 17. His father sat in the gallery, leaning forward with hands clasped, another one of his sons consoling him with a hand on his back.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht will face a minimum prison sentence of five years and maximum of up to 40 years.

Rinderknecht was being tried for a second time, after a federal jury in June deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal. U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang ordered that there be no reference to the first trial and instructed the second jury to disregard a defense witness' mention of it during his testimony.

Steve Haney, Rinderknecht's defense attorney for both trials, said they planned to appeal Friday's verdict.

"We are disappointed in the verdict, but respect the jury process," Haney said. "After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration."

Despite the jury's lean toward acquittal over the summer, prosecutors vowed to retry Rinderknecht, who has remained in custody since his arrest in October 2025. Earlier this year, prosecutors obtained a revised indictment that narrowed the scope of one charge to focus solely on damage from the initial Lachman fire, while a second count still sought to hold him responsible for both the Lachman and Palisades fires.

The secondary inferno erupted on Jan. 7, 2025, killed 12 people, destroyed 6,500 structures across the Palisades and Malibu, and caused billions of dollars in damage and insurance claims.

The top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, said the indictment was narrowed for the second trial in order to persuade jurors who might have been torn about holding Rinderknecht accountable for the Palisades fire.

Essayli said he believed the jury in the first trial "considered things that were not within the record," which led to the mistrial.

"We had to take another shot at trying this, because of the weight of the evidence," Essayli said. "There's no way we're going to let this guy walk out of the courtroom knowing he started the Palisades fire."

A juror who spoke to reporters after the verdict Friday said the strongest evidence was Rinderknecht's interview with federal investigators, when he said that he "didn't smell a fire, didn't see fireworks" on the hill before the Lachman blaze erupted.

"Everything kind of started to point towards one conclusion," said the juror, who asked to be identified only by his first name, Cameron.

A 30-year-old college student, Cameron said that without evidence proving another cause of the fire, "logically things started pointing towards [Rinderknecht]," he said.

Cameron said after the case went to the jury, it took a vote to gauge where everyone stood. Ten jurors voted guilty, one was unsure and Cameron was the sole one who voted not guilty.

"We just kept going on and on and on and just asked every question, are we going to be right about this because it's a person's life," he said.

Ultimately, Cameron said, the evidence persuaded him to vote guilty: "We decided he had to have been the one on that hill, he had to have been the one to start the fire."

Rinderknecht's second trial was contentious, with prosecutors accusing a defense witness of perjury, the defense attempting to introduce a new witness at the eleventh hour to bolster their theory of fireworks, and constant sniping between the two sides.

In closing arguments Wednesday, Assistant U.S. Atty. Mark Williams told jurors that Rinderknecht was "mad at everything and frustrated" when he hiked to a clearing overlooking Pacific Palisades and set a fire on New Year's Eve 2024. Williams said investigators ruled out fireworks as a cause "because there was no evidence to prove it."

"This fire was an incendiary fire started by an open flame," he said. "The defendant is the only one who could have started it. ... He was angry that night and he set the fire and watched it burn."

Williams also reminded the jury that it was not to consider the adequacy of the Los Angeles Fire Department's fire suppression efforts, something jurors raised following the June mistrial. In a civil lawsuit against the city and the state, Los Angeles firefighters testified about a series of communication failures and questionable decisions by higher-ups that led crews to leave the area of the New Year's Day fire prematurely.

"This case is about arson, the fire that the defendant started — not about first responders who responded to it," Williams said.

In his closing argument, Haney said jurors were "to decide the case based on the evidence," not on anything his client did "outside of the act of arson." He argued that no one saw his client start the fire and that the ignition wasn't captured in thousands of photos and videos reviewed by investigators.

Haney said investigators concluded in August 2025 that an open flame started the fire. Rinderknecht was charged that October, but Haney said authorities didn't request lab tests to prove a lighter could have ignited the fire until the following year.

"The decision came first, the test came 11 months later," Haney said. "Decided, charged and tested. That's backwards."

Mayor Karen Bass released a statement in response to the conviction that said, "No verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured."

"So many are still struggling to rebuild," Bass said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."

Essayli said the verdict against Rinderknecht does not "exonerate the city or any other actors in how they responded to the fire," noting that the Los Angeles Fire Department faces civil litigation over its handling of the 2025 wildfires.

The question of whether the city and its agencies can be held legally responsible "will be determined in other venues and other places," Essayli said. "Both things can be true — you can have an arsonist and you can have a less than adequate response by the fire department."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

Jonathan Rinderknecht was arrested Oct. 7, 2025, in Florida on suspicion of sparking the deadly Palisades fire that killed 12 people and destroyed much of the community. (U.S. Attorney's Office)

articles.title: Iraqi security forces deploy in Iran-backed militia stronghold
articles.summary: JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq — Iraqi security forces deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group, on Friday under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of Iran’s most powerful Shi’ite militia ally in the country without provoking a confrontation.
articles.body: JURF AL-SAKHAR, Iraq — Iraqi security forces deployed in Jurf al-Sakhar, a stronghold of the Kataib Hezbollah armed group, on Friday under a deal that seeks to limit the reach of Iran’s most powerful Shi’ite militia ally in the country without provoking a confrontation. Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi this week ordered security forces to move against the heavily armed Kataib Hezbollah, which officials accused of running an oil smuggling network siphoning state-owned oil worth hundreds of millions of dollars in Jurf al-Sakhar. The hardline Kataib Hezbollah (Battalions of the Party of God), branded a terrorist group by the United States, has rejected the smuggling accusations, which have led to arrests that prompted fears of an armed response. The group is among those that have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran. A convoy of vehicles flying Iraqi flags headed into Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday and soldiers took up positions in the center after senior security officials told a press conference that government forces would protect the town. Members of the Kataib Hezbollah group stood near their group’s flags. “From Jurf al-Sakhar, we begin asserting state authority across all of Iraq, confronting corruption and weapons beyond state control,” Zaidi told government troops who entered the town, speaking from a military operations center in Baghdad. “Our decision is firm: No weapons outside state authority, no weapons but Iraq‘s, no decisions but Iraq‘s, and no flag shall fly higher than the Iraqi flag.” Under the arrangement, brokered by Shi’ite politicians, Kataib members were expected to withdraw to other parts of Iraq, a major oil producer and ally of both the US and Iran. “God willing, things will be safe and secure with the presence of the security forces,” said resident Mohamed Ali. Senior Iranian representative visited Baghdad, sources say The deal will include the opening of a security headquarters in Jurf al-Sakhar on Saturday to oversee the handover. Iraq‘s energy police have begun securing an oil pipeline in Jurf al-Sakhar, the state news agency reported. “Today is a historic moment in which the Iraqi Armed Forces prove that they are the nation’s shield, safety valve, and the guardian ensuring security stability for the Iraqi people,” Sabah al-Numan, spokesperson for the commander-in-chief of the Iraqi armed forces, told the press conference. Reflecting the sensitivity of the situation, Iraqi Shi’ite political figures said Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards’ Quds Force, arrived in Baghdad on Monday to help defuse tensions with Kataib Hezbollah. So far, nine senior security and oil officials have been dismissed following an investigation focused on Jurf al-Sakhar in Babil province, about 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad. Any direct confrontation with Iran’s heavily armed militia allies in Iraq could be risky. After one of Zaidi’s predecessors ordered a similar crackdown on those armed groups five years ago, the prime minister’s Baghdad home was hit in a drone strike that authorities described at the time as an assassination attempt. Refusal to disarm US President Donald Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck US troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in solidarity with Tehran since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in February. Kataib Hezbollah and other militias, all of whom report directly to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, have refused to hand over their weapons to the state. Founded in the aftermath of the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq, Kataib is among the most influential members of the Islamic Resistance in Iraq, the umbrella group of hardline Shi’ite armed organisations supported by Iran. Kataib Hezbollah quickly developed a reputation for deadly attacks against military and diplomatic targets during the US-led counterinsurgency war and sectarian conflict of the 2000s, using snipers, rockets, mortars and roadside bombs. Wide Iranian sway in Iraq Since the 2003 US-led invasion toppled Iran’s arch-enemy, longtime Sunni leader Saddam Hussein, Tehran has steadily expanded its influence in Iraq through close ties with heavily armed Shi’ite militias and political parties. Iraqi security officials say the militias’ arsenals include assault rifles, machineguns, anti-tank guided missiles, mortars, precision-guided rockets, armed drones and some short-range ballistic and cruise missile capabilities. Kataib has its own political party, called Huquq, or Rights, with five lawmakers. An Iraqi official report said the group also generates cash through businesses such as construction, housing, trade, tourism and currency exchange, though Kataib denies this and says it is dedicated to security. Pro-Iranian militias, including Kataib, enjoy a semi-official status in Iraq, which critics say encourages them to act with impunity. A shadowy group with no announced leadership structure, Kataib Hezbollah has thousands of hardened fighters. It forms several battalions in Iraq‘s Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), a grouping of armed factions set up in 2014 to fight Islamic State and subsequently recognized as an official security force. Fighters receive state salaries and Kataib Hezbollah members, including some designated as terrorists by the US, hold senior positions in the PMF. While it is technically under the command of Iraq‘s prime minister as part of the PMF, the group often operates outside the chain of command.

President Trump has pressured Zaidi to disarm the militias that have struck U.S. troops and facilities in Saudi Arabia & the United Arab Emirates. Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg via Getty

articles.title: FOX News Media kicks off holiday season with seventh annual All-American Christmas Tree Lighting
articles.summary: It’s beginning to look a lot like Christmas in Midtown Manhattan after FOX News Media kicked off the holiday season with the All-American Christmas Tree Lighting Friday.
articles.body: It’s beginning to look a lot like Christmas in Midtown Manhattan after FOX News Media kicked off the holiday season with the All-American Christmas Tree Lighting Friday. Fox News hosts Emily Compagno, Harold Ford Jr., Greg Gutfeld, Dana Perino and Jesse Watters were joined by first lady Melania Trump for the seventh annual All-American Christmas Tree Lighting during a special edition of "The Five." The first lady helped decorate the tree before enjoying cookies and hot chocolate with the children in attendance during the festive Christmas celebration. "The Five" co-hosts reminisced on their favorite holiday memories and traditions, and the gathered children shared their Christmas wish lists. Trump said "world peace" is at the top of her Christmas wish list this year after she successfully secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the city of Oleshky in late October. FOX NEWS MEDIA CEO SUZANNE SCOTT RINGS NASDAQ CLOSING BELL AS NETWORK CELEBRATES 30TH ANNIVERSARY "I really would like to have more ceasefire. We could do it very fast if both Ukraine and Russia are willing," the first lady told Fox News. "Maybe we will have another ceasefire before Christmas." Trump called the Oleshky ceasefire a "big success" that rescued hundreds of civilians from violence while expressing hope that those affected will have a great Christmas. The first lady also spoke about her Be Best Fostering the Future initiative, which aims to empower and support children in foster care. She shared a message about the support she hopes Americans will extend to foster children during the holiday season. "They need support. They need warmth," Trump said. "They need, of course, also financial support, because once they are 18 years old, they are on their own. And that's where my focus is, Fostering the Future. "We are doing a fantastic job, and we just keep going," she continued. "So, let's hope everybody has a great Christmas and actually a warm home for everybody. That's very important." MELANIA TRUMP DETAILS HANDS-ON ROLE IN UKRAINE CEASEFIRE THAT EVACUATED NEARLY 800 CIVILIANS Trump, who oversees the White House’s Christmas decorations, also discussed this year’s theme, "America in Bloom," revealing the Christmas tree arrives at Pennsylvania Avenue on Monday. The first lady, alongside Watters, Compagno and Ford Jr., handed out ornaments for children to place them on the tree while asking the kids what was on their Christmas list. FOX News Media’s All-American Christmas Tree stands at 50 feet tall and is decorated with 18,000 ornaments and 340,000 warm white, true white and red lights. The tree features a six-foot dove topper with 4,800 embedded lights created by American Christmas, a holiday lighting and display company based in Mount Vernon, New York. The All-American Christmas Tree Lighting, sponsored by Ace Hardware, included a live performance by Phil Wickham and a blessing by Rev. Franklin Graham and "The Chosen" actor Jonathan Roumie. articles.title: Zoo shares autopsy findings following Fiona the hippo’s heartbreaking death
articles.summary: Cincinnati Zoo’s director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger, said a postmortem examination has revealed where the hat was lodged inside Fiona’s digestive tract.
articles.body: The Cincinnati Zoo on Friday released new autopsy findings after the death of Fiona, the hippo whose battle after swallowing a visitor's hat left people across the nation heartbroken. A postmortem examination determined that a foreign object, confirmed to be a hat zoo officials said was accidentally thrown into her enclosure, was lodged deep inside the hippo's massive digestive tract, according to the zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger. The hat was located halfway through the small intestine, about 25 feet from the beginning of her intestinal tract and 50 feet from where it would have exited her body as waste. FIONA THE HIPPO HONORED BY US SENATE IN UNANIMOUS RESOLUTION PRAISING CINCINNATI ZOO STAFF The findings settle lingering questions about the hat's exact location after care teams spent days trying to locate it using various methods, including ultrasounds and upper and lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopies. Care teams even obtained 9-foot-long endoscopy tools but were still unable to reach her intestines through her mouth. "The upper GI endoscopy couldn't even reach out of her large sacculated stomach," Wenninger said. BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT "Given her anatomy and the attachments from her intestinal tract to body wall, there's no place, no way to get in there with specialized endoscopes," he added. The hat's location and Fiona's anatomy also made surgical removal impossible, Wenninger said, explaining that even laparoscopic procedures, in which a scope is inserted into the abdomen through a small incision, were not feasible. "Laparoscopic surgery wasn't possible given the location and a laparotomy, so (an) open incision in a hippo that size with an incision that's that long would have been a death sentence for her," he said. Zoo officials added that the findings confirm the care team did everything possible, and the complications left no viable options for additional operations. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said. Following Fiona's death, the facility said the zoo remains open, but the area around the Hippo Cove enclosure will be closed through the weekend to give the animal care team the space it needs during this time. "Keepers, vets, staff and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss. She meant a lot to a lot of people," the zoo said in a statement. FUN FACT: FIONA THE HIPPO BECAME THE SMALLEST NILE HIPPO KNOWN TO SURVIVE While most hippos in captivity live up to 50 years, Fiona was just 9 years old when her condition rapidly deteriorated in November. She first made headlines in 2017 after defying the odds as a premature hippo. She was born six weeks early, weighing just 29 pounds. By comparison, healthy newborn hippos typically weigh between 50 and 120 pounds at birth. articles.title: USDA releases decades of Bigfoot files, including 1982 Forest Service investigation in Washington state
articles.summary: The USDA's Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records include an official 1982 Forest Service probe into footprints in Washington state's Umatilla National Forest.
articles.body: The Trump administration has slowly released a trove of government documents about one of the biggest and most enduring mysteries in American folklore: Bigfoot. On Oct. 15, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) released three files from its "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records," The Washington Post first reported, adding fresh intrigue to the legend of the towering, hair-covered creature said to roam North American forests without ever being captured. NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS The records include an official U.S. Forest Service (USFS) investigation from June 1982 into reported Bigfoot footprints discovered in the Mill Creek Watershed of Washington state's Umatilla National Forest. Investigators documented track measurements, took color photographs and made plaster casts across several field sites to preserve the unusual physical evidence. NEW JERSEY COUPLE REPORT SEEING 8-FOOT TALL BIGFOOT STEPPING OUT IN FRONT OF THEIR CAR: 'WE KNOW WHAT WE SAW' Another file details a reported encounter with the creature in Montana dating back to the 1940s. Separately, USFS staff once hosted a Bigfoot in Your Backyard forum in California's Stanislaus National Forest to discuss local sightings, noting at the time the agency could neither confirm nor deny the creature's existence. A six-page document included in last month's release, which was written in 1980, recounts a historical report from Petty Creek, Montana, by Leo Kinney, who described spotting a large set of tracks alongside three hunters in the 1940s. FOLLOW US ON X "At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was, and though we didn't confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs," Kinney wrote. The release also includes details of a 2003 sighting in Sanders County, Montana. IDAHO DEER HUNTER REPORTS BIGFOOT ENCOUNTER IN REMOTE WOODS AFTER HE 'SMELLS THE SMELL' In an interview with The Washington Post, Jeremiah Byron of the "Bigfoot Society" questioned the timing of the federal disclosures. "Why is all this cryptid and Bigfoot-related stuff happening now?" Byron asked. "I’m hoping what this means is that they could be ramping up government entities to start releasing information." While Bigfoot lore has traditionally centered on the Pacific Northwest, the creature has also surfaced in pop culture, with players reporting sightings in the video game Grand Theft Auto VI. Gamers have shared clips of the cryptid wandering the woods of Leonida, a fictional U.S. state based on Florida, before sprinting away in a panic when spotted, according to GameSpot. articles.title: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm
articles.summary: The sleeping bag’s neck hole was far too big, meaning Emma's baby daughter could wriggle down and it could cover her face.
articles.body:
Sales of a baby sleeping bag have been halted in the UK by fashion retail chain Next, after a new mum raised the alarm over its safety.

Emma Hunter, 29 from Norwich, contacted BBC Your Voice to say she realised the neck hole was far too big - meaning her daughter Rosie could potentially wriggle down, burying her face and risking suffocation.

Emma recalls: "I woke up my husband and we both agreed there was no way we could put Rosie in it."

Next says its own-brand, 2.5 tog pink floral sleep bag with removable sleeves that comes in three sizes, has been removed from the website and stores and a product recall is under way.

Next will contact and advise customers who purchased the item from them.

A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."

Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.

According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.

They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."

To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.

For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.

Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.

After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.

"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"

Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.

Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.

She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.

"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.

"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"

Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.

But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.

The Lullaby Trust is a UK charity that works to prevent sudden, unexpected infant deaths, including SIDS.

CEO Jenny Ward told BBC News that the charity could not comment on the safety of specific products, since it does not carry out independent product safety testing.

But she encourages families to check that any product they use has passed the necessary safety checks and meets British Safety Standards.

She said: "Remember to follow the manufacturer's instructions and if a family is worried about any product we would say to stop using it and contact the manufacturer.

"We support the Office for Product Safety and Standards' recent warning on certain baby sleep bags and would urge families to ensure a sleep bag fits well before they use it."

People can check if any products have been recalled by visiting the OPSS website .

articles.title: James Bond: Could Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney or Jodie Comer be the next Bond girl opposite Robert Pattinson?
articles.summary: Pattinson’s announcement as 007 has completely upped the game, and commentators say his leading lady will need a "very strong identity".
articles.body:
After months of speculation, we finally have a new Bond. The question now is - who will play Robert Pattinson’s leading lady?

What’s clear is that Pattinson’s announcement as 007 has completely upped the game.

He's one of Hollywood's biggest stars, so all eyes are on Amazon MGM to see whether they also go for an equally big name for a "Bond girl", or if they'll take a chance on someone a little less well known.

Whoever is cast opposite him, though, needs to have a "very strong identity of her own", believes film critic Larushka Ivan-Zadeh - "someone distinctive, sexy, complicated".

Showbiz reporter Catrina Rose agrees: "I'd love to see a Bond girl who's just as interesting and unpredictable as he is."

And then, some say the whole concept of a Bond girl is outdated and the role needs to evolve for a new era. So what can we expect?

No actress has yet confirmed they're in the running - but stars who have been bandied about the internet include Zendaya , whose name shot to the top of the list after Pattinson's casting.

The duo have already shared three films together this year, and make a "really exciting pairing," says Ivan-Zadeh.

Rose agrees that as one of the most recognisable actresses in Hollywood, Zendaya is "definitely someone I'd be thinking about now".

But her Euphoria co-stars Hunter Schafer and Sydney Sweeney could give her a run for her money.

There have been rumours about Sweeney getting the role for months, and you can see why, says Dr Llewella Chapman, a film historian at the University of East Anglia. "She has sex appeal and an ability to take on tougher roles too," she tells the BBC.

Sweeney was given a boost last month by former Bond girl Trina Parks, who told the Telegraph she would fit the role well because Bond needed a woman with "ownership over her sexuality".

Speculation is also growing over Pattinson’s partner, actor and singer Suki Waterhouse . She once said she’d love to play " a bad-ass Bond girl ".

But there isn’t a precedent for husband-wife couples in the films, and it may be more likely that she picks up a cameo role, if indeed she wants to.

Meanwhile, TV presenter Maya Jama has picked up new interest following her storming run on Celebrity Traitors. After she quit Love Island , rumours swirled that she could be the next Bond girl - but she’s just signed a Netflix deal, so it’s unclear if that would still be a possibility.

Another strong contender is Florence Pugh who, like Zendaya, also stars alongside Pattinson in Dune: Part Three. Earlier this week she threw her hat in the ring to be in the new Bond film - although as a villain, rather than his leading lady.

"She ticks quite a few boxes if they're looking for someone bankable," says Rose. "I could absolutely see her as a Bond woman who turns out to be the villain, someone Bond thinks is on his side, but she's actually been playing him the whole time."

Queen's Gambit star Anya Taylor-Joy is another name Amazon MGM could be thinking about if they want a big, recognisable actress, as well as Killing Eve's Jodie Comer (Villanelle meets Bond, anyone?)

Meanwhile, Crazy Rich Asians star Gemma Chan told Variety she was "flattered" by fans speculating she could be a Bond girl. "Absolutely I would," she said .

Other names that have been floated include and Ambika Mod .

And it could easily be someone totally different. Producers have previously chosen a Bond girl who isn't particularly famous yet - or is on the cusp of stardom.

But then there’s the wider question of whether the whole idea of a “Bond girl” is now somewhat outdated.

Historically, the character had little agency and existed primarily as Bond's romantic interest - and the term "girl" itself is also criticised for infantilising women.

Monica Bellucci rejected the label. She told the Guardian ahead of her appearance in Sceptre in 2015: "I can't say I'm a Bond girl because I'm too mature to be a Bond girl. I say Bond lady; Bond woman."

The way the films have treated Bond girls "hasn't always aged well", says Rose.

Some scenes from 1960s Bond films are "basically rape", and "wouldn't fly today", said No Time To Die director Cary Fukunaga in 2021 - referring to Thunderball and Goldfinger.

In reality, we have come a long way since then.

Over the years, producers have taken steps to usher the franchise into the modern era.

These days, the women of Bond are now much more likely to be sharp, capable equals to 007 - and what's defined as "attractive" has also evolved.

Belluci's inclusion in Spectre as a "Bond woman" aged 50 was widely praised for spotlighting a different type of sex appeal (even though she was only four years older than Daniel Craig in real life).

We've also had other powerful women in Bond, such as Michelle Yeoh's Colonel Wai Lin and Lashana Lynch's MI6 agent Nomi, who also made history as the first black female 007 .

Rather than fitting the traditional Bond girl mould, both of them were competent women who could give Bond a run for his money.

"We've moved away from the role being someone with a silly name and for Bond to pat on their bottom," says film critic Ivan-Zadeh. "It's moving in the right direction".

Many people say, however, there is still further to go.

Having more female Bond villains, as well as love interests, could be one way to make it more equal, suggests Rose. "That's what I'd want to see."

"They can be romantic interests, villains, spies, allies or even the person who ultimately outsmarts Bond. There's room for all of those roles,” agrees showbiz journalist Nikki Onafuye.

Another way the roles could evolve is by bringing in "a queer or sexually fluid Bond woman," says Ivan-Zadeh. "Someone whose desires don’t simply revolve around Bond. That would create some genuinely interesting chemistry.”

Others are hoping to see more diverse actresses cast from film markets such as China, India or Nigeria.

“There have been a number of women of colour in the past, but I'd like to see more," says Be Manzini, writer and film-maker.

"I'd like to see an Indian Bond girl," agrees Chapman. "Aishwarya Rai was touted for the follow up to Die Another Day but never got there."

More broadly, there is an appetite to see Bond girls have their own lives.

“For me, it's about giving these women proper storylines,” says Onafuye. "They should have their own motivations and their own ambitions.”

None of this is to say we should do away with the traditional Bond glamour.

"No-one wants to see Bond girls slumping around in their PJs," says Ivan-Zadeh.

But the important distinction is that "being sexy shouldn't be the only thing a female character has to offer,” says Onafuye.

“To those arguing that it's fine for Bond's women just to be sexy and hot, I'd say there's nothing sexier or hotter than a woman (or man) with a brain and a wit,” adds entertainment journalist Caroline Frost.

Ultimately, whatever direction the new producers go in, most agree the "Bond girl" or Bond woman is a key part of the Bond universe.

But continuing to evolve is crucial, says Chapman. "It's about retaining the humour and history of Bond but also recognising - this is 2026."

There are, of course, lots of other women within the films, and for Frost, the key is to have a range of different Bond women on screen, "all well matched with 007 in terms of strength, resources and, above all, wit".

"Bond has always had fascinating women," agrees Rose. "I'd just love the next film to give them the space to be as interesting as the man in the tuxedo."

articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers: Fans use art to visualise phone-free concert era
articles.summary: The American singer has brought in a no-phone policy for the shows, inspiring fans to explore their artistic talent.
articles.body:
Phoebe Bridgers has drawn in fans over the years with her raw, vulnerable lyrics and indie sound that can make even the messiest emotions feel less lonely.

The US artist's third album Lost Weekend, released this summer after a six-year wait, delves into falling in and out of love, grappling with change and the confusing feelings that come with grief.

On her tour of the Grammy-nominated record, Bridgers has introduced a no-phone policy - a move that's had an unexpected side effect.

Instead of taking photos and videos of the shows, some are creating artwork as a reminder of the gigs.

Massive Bridgers fan Olivia MacDonald, from Massachusetts, attended the singer's show in Boston last month.

She was initially "shocked" by the no-phone rule, as employed by artists including Bob Dylan and Jack White, but became a convert.

Without the distraction of phones, she says, fans chatted, danced and sang along with each other.

"Once I got to the concert, I realised this is such a unique way to connect and bring everybody together," she says.

MacDonald, a pen and ink artist, brought her sketchbook along to the show after spotting fellow fans' interpretations on social media.

She relived the gig by drawing standout moments such as Bridgers' dripping, electric blue eye make-up and her guitar, originally owned by the late American musician Elliott Smith.

"Everybody takes away something different," says 28-year-old MacDonald.

"That's the beauty of it, that everybody can have a different interpretation."

Sharing her designs on social media helped her connect with other fans, who reached out to discuss their experiences of the show.

"I feel like with photos or videos, you capture a moment in time, and with drawings, you really capture a feeling and people can connect to that feeling," she says.

Bridgers has navigated an emotional whirlwind since she was propelled to stardom with the release of her emotionally charged and critically acclaimed album Punisher in 2020.

The 32-year-old Californian has toured and won three Grammys with supergroup Boygenius, lived out a high-profile romance and breakup with Irish actor Paul Mescal, and lost her dad in 2023.

Fans believe she explores some of these experiences in her latest album.

MacDonald says Bridgers explained to the Boston crowd that the no-phone rule would allow her to talk openly with her audience like friends, without the worry of those moments ending up online.

Some fans expressed worries the policy could exclude people with disabilities or those who might need to contact someone in an emergency.

MacDonald says she shared the reservations, but points out fans were able to keep their phones on them and access the sealed pouches they were stored in at special designated areas inside the venue.

Fan Anna Meyer, who attended the New York show, agrees the device-free aspect made the show a better experience for artist and audience, and allowed the special lighting effects to be fully appreciated without being distorted by phone lights.

The graphic designer, 35, chose to capture this element afterwards - focusing on a poignant moment when a kneeling Bridgers played piano in the glow of a spotlight.

"It was so cathartic to feel so inspired," she says.

"And I do wonder, if I did have my phone, would I have felt this need to sit down and immediately draw something from the show?"

Meyer feels the trend is particularly special as it's put a focus on techniques, such as pen and paper, in an age when traditional art feels under threat.

"We're now in an era of AI where they want us to believe if you want to create something visual, you have to use a computer and AI programme," she says.

"We all have the ability to create, and our own creations that come from our own mind and hand are far better than anything that a computer can create.

"And sometimes even far better than anything that a camera can capture."

Followers of the new trend argue it also helps to guard against gig spoilers , where big moments go viral on social media before crowds get to see them in-person.

Lillie Collins, a fan from Michigan, feels artwork offers "a little teaser" rather than giving everything away.

The 20-year-old painted her own interpretation after seeing Bridgers' show in Detroit and her videos revealing the piece blew up on TikTok.

She says the wave of positive responses was "very exciting" as she'd never had that reaction before, and it's now made her consider that creating art could be a successful career route.

Bridgers herself appears to approve too, as her team has shared several posts praising the artworks .

MacDonald and Meyer were among those who got shout-outs on the official Lost Tour Instagram page, as was Collins, who says the idea Bridgers may have seen her artwork had her "screaming".

"I really appreciate how she was able to bring this level of creativity and humanity into her performances," she says.

Bridgers will kick off her UK run of shows at Manchester's Co-op Live on Thursday, followed by dates in Glasgow, Birmingham and London.

Ayanoh Nakamoto was one of the fans who attended a special intimate show at Union Chapel, London, where Bridgers tested the no-phone policy.

She will be back in the crowd for the first London show next month, and says the "excitement has built up so much because we haven't been able to see what is really happening in the US right now".

"It's just so cool to have an experience where it feels like it isn't spoilt for you," she says.

Despite Nakamoto running a TikTok page where she shares her concert video content, she admits it feels liberating to put her phone away and be in the moment.

She jokes she doesn't have an "artistic bone" in her body, but thinks this might be her chance to try her hand at drawing, even if it is a stick-figure sketch.

"I wonder if this is going to be a stepping stone for artists to maybe have this at more concerts and just feel that connection back to the audience in the future."

articles.title: Former UK banker Dominique Bogle turned her wig business ‘Hair Anatomy’ into a full-time career after TikTok sales neared £15,000 in one month and quit her job eight months later
articles.summary: Hair Anatomy founder Dominique Bogle, a United Kingdom banker turned wig business owner, built a full-time career from TikTok sales of almost £15,000 in
articles.body: Hair Anatomy founder Dominique Bogle, a United Kingdom banker turned wig business owner, built a full-time career from TikTok sales of almost £15,000 in one month and quit her banking job eight months later. Her wig business began as a part-time side project, until she first went live on TikTok from her kitchen in 2022. Her story shows how TikTok live selling and social commerce can turn a phone and a stock of wigs into a full-time wig business. By 2025, the Birmingham founder was shipping orders across continents and going live on TikTok at least five days a week.How alopecia and a gap in the market led Dominique Bogle to start ‘Hair Anatomy ’, the wig businessAccording to Forbes, Bogle was 21 and midway through her undergraduate degree when she began experiencing sudden, unexplained hair loss. A few small patches quickly became a source of daily stress and insecurity. With no roadmap, she researched suppliers and ordered samples, trying everything from synthetic styles to premium human hair pieces. Finding something she could wear confidently proved difficult and expensive; human hair wigs cost at least £2,000, while the synthetic wigs of the time were poor quality and could only be worn once.Bogle, who is from Birmingham, was diagnosed with alopecia. She told the BBC that losing your hair feels like losing part of your identity, and that wigs boost confidence and make you feel like a woman again because, in her words, “as a woman your hair is everything”.At the time, she worked in corporate banking, a world far removed from beauty retail. The more she searched, the more she realised that other women were quietly facing the same problem. That gave her the idea for Hair Anatomy, a brand that sells synthetic wigs designed to move like real hair and guides customers through an overwhelming journey with understanding and care.How going live on TikTok from a kitchen in 2022 brought almost £15,000 in wig salesFor the first couple of years, Bogle sold through her website, with steady but limited traffic that came mainly from Instagram. She had initially dismissed TikTok as a dancing app not worth taking seriously, but she changed her mind in 2022. Her approach was simple: she set up her phone, showed the small stock she had on hand and directed viewers to her website.The sales that followed surprised her. Soon afterwards, she left her banking career to focus solely on Hair Anatomy, joining a growing wave of small business owners using TikTok Shop to sell directly to customers without leaving the app.How TikTok live selling, packing lives and show-and-tell sessions build a loyal wig communityBogle’s live sessions fall into two kinds. Morning packing lives with the fulfilment team let customers watch orders being wrapped in real time, while evening show-and-tell sessions demonstrate wigs and answer questions. Together they add up to a minimum of four hours on each live day. That consistency and variety keep her audience engaged and help new viewers discover the brand through TikTok’s For You page.The real draw is the personal connection. articles.summary: LIMA, Peru — A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck central Peru on Friday, the German Research Centre for Geosciences said, sending some in the capital Lima into the streets, though there were no immediate reports of casualties or significant damage.
articles.body: LIMA, Peru — A magnitude 6.8 earthquake struck central Peru on Friday, the German Research Centre for Geosciences said, sending some in the capital Lima into the streets, though there were no immediate reports of casualties or significant damage. The quake, which was felt in the capital Lima, struck in the Andean region of Junin at a depth of 129 km, according to Peru‘s Geophysical Institute. In Lima, residents evacuated their homes, and television footage showed lawmakers leaving Congress. Vicente Quispe, a local council member in Junin province, about 320 km (200 miles) east of Lima, told local broadcaster RPP that the authorities had not received reports of damage following the strong tremor. “So far, no damage has been reported. This is the first time an earthquake of this magnitude has been felt in this area,” he said. Junin is home to several midsize mining operations as well as the Chinalco-owned Toromocho mine, one of Peru‘s largest copper mines. Peru is the world’s third-largest copper producer, and mining is a key driver of the economy. The US Tsunami Warning System said there was no tsunami threat following the earthquake. Peru lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a seismically active zone where tectonic plate movements frequently trigger quakes.

articles.title: They were fined $811m for conning migrants - the scams didn't stop
articles.summary: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.
articles.body:
Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.

But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.

Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.

The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.

But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.

"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.

"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."

Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.

It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.

Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.

Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.

Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.

A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.

Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.

Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.

Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.

But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.

A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.

But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.

"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."

Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.

"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"

Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.

The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.

The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.

In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.

Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.

As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.

Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.

Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.

This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.

A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.

Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.

A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.

Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.

Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.

When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.

She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.

An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".

"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."

They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.

But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

articles.title: A Florida man pleaded guilty in a $42 million Medicare fraud case involving medical equipment and genetic tests; prosecutors say the proceeds funded a 47-foot yacht and luxury vehicles
articles.summary: A healthcare fraud operation allegedly built on unnecessary medical equipment, questionable genetic testing and millions of dollars in fraudulent
articles.body: A healthcare fraud operation allegedly built on unnecessary medical equipment, questionable genetic testing and millions of dollars in fraudulent insurance claims has ended in a guilty plea, with investigators uncovering a trail of extravagant purchases along the way. A Florida businessman who allegedly helped orchestrate the multimillion-dollar scheme used the proceeds to finance an expensive lifestyle, including a yacht worth more than $600,000 and several luxury vehicles. The case has now entered the sentencing stage, bringing renewed attention to federal efforts to tackle fraud involving taxpayer-funded healthcare programmes.Florida businessman admits role in $42 million Medicare fraudAccording to the Office of Public Affairs, U.S. Department of Justice, Chad Monroe, 48, of Tarpon Springs, Florida, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud and wire fraud in connection with a scheme involving approximately $42 million in fraudulent Medicare-related activity. Court documents revealed that Monroe worked with several individuals to submit false claims for durable medical equipment and cancer genetic testing that beneficiaries neither needed nor requested.The equipment included knee, wrist, ankle and back braces. Prosecutors said the operation relied on three medical supply businesses: Maksix Medical Products Inc., Orthotech Atlanta LLC and 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC. Through these companies, Monroe and his associates allegedly submitted more than $26 million in fraudulent claims to Medicare, Medicare Advantage plans and TRICARE.Illegal kickbacks allegedly fuelled medical testing schemeThe Justice Department stated that Monroe attempted to conceal his involvement in the businesses by directing associates to provide misleading information on Medicare enrollment documents. Another important component of the operation involved obtaining medical orders for equipment and genetic testing. According to the Office of Public Affairs, U.S. Department of Justice, Monroe paid illegal kickbacks to purported telemedicine companies to generate doctors' orders that could support the claims. He also operated through a company called Health and Life Networking LLC, which allegedly sold genetic testing orders to laboratories involved in the scheme. Those laboratories reportedly paid Monroe more than $15 million in illegal kickbacks in exchange for the orders. Investigators said the arrangements helped generate fraudulent billing activity involving medical services and products that beneficiaries did not require.Fraud proceeds allegedly financed yacht and luxury carsBeyond the healthcare scheme, prosecutors uncovered evidence of spending that illustrated how the alleged proceeds were used. The Office of Public Affairs, U.S. Department of Justice, reported that Monroe purchased a 47-foot yacht named The Rogue Shark, valued at more than $600,000. He also acquired a Cadillac Escalade and other luxury vehicles using money generated through the fraudulent activities. Authorities have seized the yacht along with more than $1 million in additional assets connected to the case.Monroe also admitted involvement in a separate attempt to obtain federal financial assistance fraudulently. He directed an associate to submit a Paycheck Protection Program loan application worth more than $30,000 using misleading information about the ownership of 1st Choice Medical Supply LLC.Multiple federal agencies investigated the caseThe investigation involved several federal agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, the FBI, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation division. Prosecutors from the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division's Health Care Fraud Section are handling the case.The department also highlighted its broader healthcare fraud enforcement efforts. Its Health Care Fraud Strike Force Programme has charged more than 6,200 defendants since 2007 in cases involving over $45 billion in allegedly fraudulent billings to federal healthcare programmes and private insurers.Guilty plea could bring decades in prisonDespite admitting his involvement, Monroe has yet to receive a sentence. According to the Office of Public Affairs, U.S. Department of Justice, he faces a maximum of 10 years in prison for conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud and up to 30 years for wire fraud. A federal district court judge will determine the final punishment after considering sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing date has not yet been announced.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Sia, Paul Kelly and other Australian celebrities oppose a $96 million MotoGP circuit in Adelaide; the project could remove 377 parkland trees, including 42 classified as significant
articles.summary: Dozens of Australian celebrities, including Adelaide-born musicians Paul Kelly and Sia, have joined a campaign against a $96 million MotoGP circuit
articles.body: Dozens of Australian celebrities, including Adelaide-born musicians Paul Kelly and Sia, have joined a campaign against a $96 million MotoGP circuit planned for the Adelaide parklands. The first four trees were felled on Friday as part of preliminary water works, with protesters gathering behind temporary fencing. The project is expected to require the removal of 377 trees, 42 of them significant, the Adelaide Circuit Redevelopment Project website states. An open letter to Premier Peter Malinauskas has gathered more than 5,000 signatures. Environment Minister Emily Bourke said the event would bring tourism benefits, and the government has promised replacement planting.More than 5,000 sign open letter opposing the $96 million MotoGP circuitDozens of Australian celebrities have called for the tree removals for the proposed circuit to be halted. They include Adelaide-born musicians Paul Kelly and Sia, MasterChef judge Poh Ling Yeow, former Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett, and comedian and actress Magda Szubanski. They have signed an open letter to SA Premier Peter Malinauskas and the state government, which had gathered more than 5,000 signatures at the time of reporting. The letter asks the government to commit to protecting the parklands into the future.Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Poh Ling Yeow said the time to act was now. She told reporters that if the project went ahead, it would mark "one of the greatest environmental tragedies the state has seen". She added that the group was not anti-sport and acknowledged the sport's community value, saying the aim was to find a better solution.Adelaide MotoGP circuit website says 95% of parkland trees will remain untouchedAccording to the Adelaide Circuit Redevelopment Project website, the proposed circuit has been designed with care for the Adelaide Park Lands. The site says protecting significant native trees has been a priority, alongside efforts to minimise impacts on biodiversity, habitat and natural ecosystems. It states that specialists in ecology, environment, heritage and landscape architecture worked alongside engineers throughout the design process.There are currently 8,895 trees in the circuit precinct, and 95% of them will remain untouched. It states that the project is expected to require the removal of 377 trees, the majority of which are unregulated, invasive species, dead or in poor health. Of those, 42 are significant. A further 88 trees will be transplanted to nearby locations within the park in line with arborists' advice, and another 22 require further below-ground investigation to confirm they can be retained. These vegetation impacts are managed and offset under its Vegetation Impact Assessment Guideline.Environment Minister Emily Bourke defends MotoGP projectAs reported by ABC News, the 4.13-kilometre circuit for the 2027 event was proposed to be laid in Victoria Park and to cut through the parklands between Wakefield Road and Rundle Road. It described the project as costing $96 million and said it was set to remove nearly 400 trees, including 42 significant trees. The SA government has previously pledged to replace them with mature stock on a 10-to-one basis.Environment Minister Emily Bourke said everyone has a right to protest but that the MotoGP would bring tourism benefits, including filling hotel rooms, restaurants and cafes. She said the government had completed community consultation and would invest $15 million to support tree planting in the parklands. She said the government had promised to plant more than 3,000 trees to replace about 377 set to be removed. She described the morning's protests as "relatively peaceful" but said it was unfortunate to hear reports of workers being verbally abused.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: UP man takes SBI home loan in 1997, repays it in 2019; bank fails to return original deed for 7 years, consumer commission orders Rs 5,000 daily penalty and Rs 10,000 costs
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: An elderly man in Aligarh had to approach the consumer commission after the State Bank of India (SBI) failed to return his original property deed
articles.body: LUCKNOW: An elderly man in Aligarh had to approach the consumer commission after the State Bank of India (SBI) failed to return his original property deed for seven years despite the closure of his home loan. Holding the bank guilty of deficiency in service, the Aligarh District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has directed it to hand over the document and pay compensation of Rs 5,000 for every day of delay, calculated from the date the loan was repaid until the deed is returned.The complainant, Gulveer Singh Chauhan, 70, a resident of Gyan Sarovar Colony, had taken a home loan from SBI's City Branch in Baradwari in 1997. As security for the loan, he deposited the original sale deed (document number 7134), dated December 18, 1997, with the bank. Chauhan cleared the entire outstanding loan on May 13, 2019, following which the bank issued him a no-dues certificate. However, his repeated requests for the return of the original property papers did not yield any result. The bank reportedly told him that it was unable to trace the deed.The absence of the original document created problems for Chauhan in dealing with his property. He said he faced difficulties in establishing ownership, transferring the house and securing another loan from a different bank. With the matter unresolved, he filed a consumer complaint on June 13, 2023. During the proceedings, SBI acknowledged that Chauhan had taken a loan and deposited the original deed with it, but contested his complaint, describing it as false.The commission also examined a letter issued by the bank on February 13, 2020. It confirmed that the loan account had been closed on May 13, 2019, with no outstanding dues. The bench, comprising commission chairman Hasnain Qureshi and member Purnima Singh Rajput, observed that the bank's failure to return the original property document after receiving full repayment amounted to a deficiency in service.In its order, the commission directed SBI to return the original sale deed and pay Chauhan Rs 5,000 per day from May 13, 2019, until the document is handed over. The bank has also been asked to pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation expenses. It has been given 45 days to comply with the directions.
