articles.title: Before throwing away wine corks and bottle caps, try these DIY projects: Turn small discarded household materials into notice boards, coasters, miniature planters and quirky wall decor
articles.summary: Almost every kitchen has a little jar or drawer holding wine corks and bottle caps that nobody has the heart to throw out.
articles.body: Almost every kitchen has a little jar or drawer holding wine corks and bottle caps that nobody has the heart to throw out. They are small, light and oddly satisfying to hold, and it turns out they are also great craft material. Natural cork is soft, grippy and water-resistant, while metal bottle caps are sturdy and colourful. You do not need to be a skilled crafter, either. A bit of glue, some patience and an afternoon are enough to turn these odds and ends into things you will actually use and show off. Here are five easy ideas.A cork notice board for notes and remindersThis is the easiest project to begin with. Collect around 30 to 40 corks, depending on the size of the frame you want. Cut some of them in half lengthwise, then glue them onto a flat piece of cardboard or an old picture frame, arranging them in a pattern you like. Let the glue dry fully. You can push pins into the cork easily, so it works well for to-do lists, photos, bills and school timetables. It looks lovely in a study corner or kitchen and makes a thoughtful gift too.Cork coasters for your tea and coffeeCork is naturally good at soaking up moisture and protecting surfaces, which makes it perfect for coasters. Slice corks into thin rounds, about half a centimetre thick, using a sharp knife with care. Arrange the rounds in a circle or square and glue them together on a flat backing, such as felt or a thin sheet of cardboard. Once set, trim the edges so they are neat. A set of four makes a great housewarming gift. Use natural cork where possible, since some synthetic ones do not hold up well against hot cups.Miniature planters for tiny succulentsCorks can hold small plants, which makes them very cute on a windowsill or desk. Cut off a small section from the top of a cork, scoop out a little hollow with a spoon or knife, and fill it with a pinch of soil. Add a tiny succulent or a bit of moss, and water it lightly. You can also glue a small magnet to the back, so the planter sticks to the fridge. These are best for very small plants, so do not expect them to grow too large without repotting.Bottle cap wall decor that adds colourBottle caps come in bright reds, golds and blues, and they look striking when grouped together. Clean and dry them, then glue them onto a wooden board or old frame to create a mosaic, a flower, a heart or even your initials. Spray paint can give them a fresh colour if you want a more uniform look. Hang the finished piece in a balcony, game room or kitchen. Handle the caps carefully, as some have sharp edges, and ask an adult to help children with this project.Fridge magnets and small giftsFor a quick, fun finish, turn leftovers into magnets and keepsakes. Glue a small magnet to the back of a bottle cap, then stick a photo, picture or a little painted design on the front. You can also add a tiny drop of resin or clear glue over the picture for a glossy look. These make charming party favours, return gifts or personalised keepsakes. Corks can be turned into little animals or stamps, too, with a bit of paint, so you can keep experimenting with whatever you have left.Disclaimer:This article is for general informational and creative purposes only. Results may vary depending on the materials, tools and techniques used. Always handle knives, scissors, glue guns and sharp-edged bottle caps carefully, and keep them away from young children. articles.title: 'Apologise for 1962 humiliation': Rijiju fires 4 questions at Rahul over 'compromised PM' jibe
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju on Saturday hit back at Rahul Gandhi over his “compromised PM” jibe at Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju on Saturday hit back at Rahul Gandhi over his “compromised PM” jibe at Prime Minister Narendra Modi. He challenged the Congress to answer four questions on the 1962 war with China, poverty and India's economic standing under its rule, and asked whether the party would apologise for what he called the “1962 humiliation”.In a post on X, Rijiju listed the questions and referred to his village being occupied by China during the 1962 conflict.“Congress must answer 4 questions: My village was occupied by China in 1962. Will Congress apologise for the 1962 humiliation? 2. Congress kept India a poor nation. Why? 3. Why was India called the land of snake charmers? 4. Why was India's economy insulted as Hindu rate of growth?” he wrote.Rijiju's response came a day after Rahul Gandhi criticised PM Modi over a trilateral meeting involving US president Donald Trump, Chinese president Xi Jinping and Russian president Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China.Also Read| PM Modi’s remark on jobs & wages a confession: CongressSharing a photograph of the three leaders at the meeting, Rahul wrote on X, “If Congress were in power, India's Prime Minister would be sitting at this table. A compromised PM can never sit at this table.”The exchange follows Rahul's remarks at the University of Chicago on Wednesday, where he questioned India's role in international affairs and described the country as a “side player”.“India, by its size, naturally has a global voice and India should be actively involved in global conversations. But frankly, India has become a side player, while Pakistan is busy negotiating with Iran and the United States,” Rahul had said.He also said that Pakistan's support for terrorism remained a major obstacle to any dialogue between the two countries.“There is scope, but there is a major problem, and that is Pakistan’s support for and promotion of terrorism within our country. This is absolutely out of the question. It is impossible for us to accept a situation where our innocent people are being killed while we engage in talks with Pakistan. So, the moment that stops, then a conversation can potentially begin,” he said.Reacting to Rahul's “side player” remarks on Friday, Rijiju had urged him not to make statements against India, either within the country or abroad.“I have not heard him. But I would like to urge him not to say things against the country, whether he is in the country or outside,” the minister told reporters.The BJP also criticised Rahul's comments, with party leaders accusing him of undermining India's international standing. BJP national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia shared an AI-generated image depicting Rahul Gandhi serving drinks to Trump at the trilateral meeting, captioning it: “Kuch aise (Something like this)”.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Himalayan marmot droppings could help track climate change
articles.summary: BENGALURU: What can the droppings of a Himalayan marmot reveal about climate change?
articles.body: BENGALURU: What can the droppings of a Himalayan marmot reveal about climate change? Quite a bit, according to a new study that has found pollen grains, fungal spores and elemental signatures preserved in the faeces of the high-altitude herbivore can provide clues to changing vegetation and environmental conditions in the higher Himalaya.Scientists from the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), an autonomous institute under the Department of Science and Technology, explored whether marmot faeces could serve as an alternative biological archive to reconstruct environmental changes. Their findings, published in the journal PLOS One, could offer a useful tool for studying remote, arid mountain environments where conventional sources of palaeoenvironmental evidence are scarce.The Himalaya is particularly sensitive to changes in temperature, precipitation and snow cover. Such changes can affect alpine vegetation and wildlife habitats. Traditionally, scientists have relied on lake sediments, peat and soil to reconstruct past environmental conditions. The researchers sought to establish whether biological material preserved in marmot droppings could provide similar insights.The Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana) inhabits cold, dry alpine environments and depends on local vegetation for food and shelter. Pollen preserved in its faeces reflects the plants consumed by the animal, thereby offering a record of the surrounding alpine-steppe vegetation.The research team analysed faecal samples collected from two Himalayan regions, using pollen and fungal-spore identification, statistical methods and Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy coupled with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (FESEM-EDS) to determine elemental composition.The analysis identified several plant groups in the marmot's diet, including Artemisia, Asteroideae, Caryophyllaceae, Poaceae, Cyperaceae and Chenopodiaceae. Researchers also examined ratios between three pollen combinations: Artemisia/Chenopodiaceae, Artemisia/Cyperaceae and Artemisia/Ephedra. These were used to interpret vegetation patterns and associated climatic conditions.The results showed that the marmot's mixed plant-based diet was dominated by groups such as Artemisia, Asteroideae, Caryophyllaceae and Chenopodiaceae, reflecting the characteristics of alpine vegetation. The researchers concluded that the Himalayan marmot could serve as an indicator species for understanding vegetation and climate changes in the higher Himalaya.The study also found that changes in marmot habitats could indicate shifts in altitude associated with changing environmental conditions. Combining pollen, fungal spores and elemental analysis could therefore provide a modern reference for future palaeoecological studies and help reconstruct past ecological changes.The findings could have implications beyond climate research. Marmots are an important prey species for snow leopards, and a better understanding of their habitat requirements could help monitor changes in the wider ecosystem and inform wildlife conservation strategies.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
